IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
Civil Appeal  No(s).  9767/2026
@ SLP (C) No. 25293/2026
VIVEK MEHETRE & ORS.                               Appellant(s)
                                VERSUS
THE DY. REGISTRAR, COOPERATIVE SOCIETIES & ORS.  Respondent(s)
O R D E R 
  
1. Having regard to the nature of the
order that we propose to pass as also that
the second and third respondents, who are
the main contesting respondents, are already
represented, and have consented for final
disposal of this matter at the notice stage
itself, we do not propose to issue notice to
respondents 1 and 4 as it would serve no
useful purpose.
2. Leave granted.
3. This  appeal  emanates  from  a
proceeding  initiated  by  the  Deputy
Registrar,  Cooperative  Societies,  Thane
(City) under Sections 75 of the Maharashtra
1

--- Page 40 ---
Co-operative Societies Act, 1960 (for short
“the 1960 Act”).
4. The  Deputy  Registrar  initiated
proceedings under Section 75(5) of the 1960
Act on account of default on the part of the
management of the Society in complying with
the various requirements of Section 75 of
the 1960 Act. 
5. According to  the Deputy  Registrar,
notices were issued to the management and,
thereafter, the management was heard and
opportunity was given to produce documents.
In those proceedings, upon finding that the
Society had not submitted the account audit
reports and had not furnished information
regarding elections, the Deputy Registrar,
exercising its powers under Section 75(5) of
the 1960 Act, disqualified as many as seven
office bearers of the Society.
6. Aggrieved by the order of the Deputy
Registrar, instead of taking recourse to the
alternative remedy of revision under Section
154  of  the  1960  Act,  the  appellants
2

--- Page 41 ---
preferred a Writ Petition before the High
Court. By the impugned order, the High Court
dismissed the Writ Petition.
7. Aggrieved by the impugned order dated
08.07.2026, this appeal has been filed.
8. The  submission  on  behalf  of  the
appellants inter alia is that the provisions
of  Section  75  of  the  1960  Act  require
service  of  notice  before  an  action
contemplated  thereunder  could  be  taken.
There  was  no  service  of  notice  and,
therefore, the proceedings stood vitiated.
It is also the submission on behalf of the
appellants that under sub-section (5) of
Section 75 of the 1960 Act, action can be
taken against an officer or member of the
committee who without any reasonable excuse
fails to comply with the mandate of any of
the  sub-sections  of  Section  75.  It  is
submitted that there is no inquiry by the
Deputy Registrar to pin-point as to who was
in  default  in  complying  with  the
requirements of the provisions of Section
3

--- Page 42 ---
75.  In  such  circumstances,  treating  all
members of the committee liable is clearly
in violation of the spirit of sub-section
(5) of Section 75 of the 1960 Act. 
9. In addition, the learned counsel for
the appellants sought to bring to our notice
additional documents to substantiate that
there has been no default in complying with
the mandate of the provisions of Section 75.
10. In  response,  on  behalf  of  the
contesting respondents it was submitted that
a clear finding has been returned by the
Deputy Registrar that the show cause notice
was served on the members of the committee
of  the  Society.  Moreover,  they  had
participated in the hearing on various dates
mentioned in the order.  Therefore, once the
appellants  had  participated  in  the
proceedings before the Deputy Registrar and
they had ample opportunity to submit their
response as well as documents, having failed
to  submit  documents  to  show  statutory
compliances, they cannot complain that no
4

--- Page 43 ---
opportunity of hearing was provided to them.
It has also been submitted that the High
Court has been categorical on the above
aspect and has returned a clear finding that
despite opportunity, the appellants have not
submitted  documents  in  support  of  their
stand; therefore, the finding returned by
the Deputy Registrar that there was non-
compliance of the provisions of Section 75
of the 1960 Act cannot be faulted. It has
also been pointed out on behalf of the
respondents that despite an opportunity to
the appellants to withdraw the writ petition
and pursue the alternative remedy under the
Act,  they  pressed  the  writ  petition.
However, they did not produce any documents
to  successfully  question  the  findings
returned by the Deputy Registrar; therefore,
they  cannot  now  be  permitted  to  submit
additional documents in support of their
case.
11. We  have  considered  the  rival
contentions and have perused the materials
5

--- Page 44 ---
available on record.
12. Before  addressing  the  contentions
raised before us, we may take notice of the
provisions of sub-section (5) of Section 75
of the 1960 Act. Sub-section (5) of Section
75, under which action has been taken by the
Deputy Registrar, reads thus:
“(5) If default is made, in calling
a general body meeting within the
period prescribed under sub-section
(1),  or  in  complying  with  sub-
sections (2), (2A), (3), (4) the
Registrar  may by order declare any
officer or member of the committee
whose duty it was to call such a
meeting or comply with sub-section
(2), (2A), (3), (4) and who without
any  reasonable  excuse  failed  to
comply with any of the aforesaid
sub-sections disqualified for being
elected and for being any officer or
member of the committee for such
period not exceeding five years, as
he may specify in such an order and,
if the officer is a servant of the
society, impose a penalty on him to
pay an amount not exceeding five
thousand rupees. Before making an
order under this sub-section, the
Registrar shall give, or cause to be
given, a reasonable opportunity to
the person concerned showing cause
against the action proposed to be
taken in regard to him.” 
(Emphasis supplied)  
13. A  bare  reading  of  the  aforesaid
provision would indicate that action is to
6

--- Page 45 ---
be  taken  against  the  person  who  was
responsible  for  non-compliance  and  who
without any reasonable excuse had failed to
comply  with  the  mandate  of  any  of  the
specified sub-sections of Section 75.
14. The order of the Deputy Registrar,
though records a finding that there has been
non-compliance  of  the  requirements  of
specified sub-sections of Section 75, does
not  record  any  finding  as  to  who  was
responsible  for  such  compliances.  The
relevant portion of the order of the Deputy
Registrar is extracted below:
“It is mentioned regarding this. In
the present case, it appears that
the  members  were  deprived  of
transparency, scrutiny or democratic
control. Similarly, it is seen that
it  happened  repeatedly.  Under
Section  75,  for  each  sub-clause
under sub-,clause (1) holding the
meeting,  under  sub-clause  (2)
placing  the  accounts,  under  sub-
clause (2A) appointing the auditor,
under sub-clause (3) submission of
the  report,  under  sub-clause  (4)
considering  the  surplus  profit
distribution, regarding this, from
the  perspective  of  public
accountability and transparency, it
is  necessary  to  hold  the  office
bearers of the society responsible
as  per  the  provisions  of  the
7

--- Page 46 ---
Maharashtra  Co-operative  Societies
Act 1960 and the approved bylaws.
Therefore,  for  the  failure  to
perform the duties of the office
bearers of the society for the years
2015- 2016, and for not complying
with Section 75(2), 75(4) and Rule
98, 138, 139 and 140 of the approved
bylaws, the following members Shri.
Satish Pande - Chairman, Shri. Vivek
Mehete - Secretary, Mrs. H. N. Lohar
- Treasurer and other members are
held responsible and it would be
appropriate to disqualify them for a
period  of  02  years  as  per  the
provision under Section 75(5) of the
Maharashtra  Co-operative  Societies
Act 1960. The office has come to
this conclusion.”
15. We, therefore, find substance in the
submissions made on behalf of the appellants
that there has been no discussion in the
order passed by the Deputy Registrar as
regards  who  was  responsible  for  non-
compliance of the provisions of Section 75
of the 1960 Act.
16. Insofar as the submission regarding
non-service of notice is concerned, we find
that  the  Deputy  Registrar  had  not  only
considered the response submitted by the
appellants but has put on record that they
were heard on multiple occasions. Once it is
8

--- Page 47 ---
borne  out  from  the  record  that  the
appellants  had  the  occasion  to  file  a
response and were heard and their response
was considered, they cannot fall back on the
question  of  service  of  notice.  To  this
extent, the High Court was correct in its
view that the appellants cannot complain
about violation of the principles of natural
justice. 
17. At this stage, we may also observe
that as per the recital in the order of the
Deputy Registrar, notices were sent. In such
circumstances,  when  the  Deputy  Registrar
records in its order that notices were sent
and, thereafter, responses were received and
the noticees were heard, the ground that
they  were  not  afforded  opportunity  of
hearing cannot be sustained. 
18. We may also observe that the Deputy
Registrar as well as the High Court has
taken notice of the fact that no documents
were produced on behalf of the appellants to
substantiate compliance of the requirements
9

--- Page 48 ---
of various sub-sections of Section 75 of the
1960 Act. In such circumstances, an action
under sub-section (5) of Section 75 of the
1960 Act was warranted.
19. However, what is important is that
action under sub-section (5) of Section 75
of the 1960 Act is to be taken against the
person who is responsible for the default.
Here we notice that the action has been
taken against all members of the committee
and  not  against  those  who  have  been
identified as responsible for non-compliance
of  the  provisions.  Therefore,  to  this
extent,  we  deem  it  appropriate  to  give
liberty to the appellants to file a revision
before the revisional authority in terms of
the provisions of Section 154 of the 1960
Act.  If  any  such  revision  is  preferred
within one month from today, the same shall
be accorded due consideration limited to the
question  of  culpability/responsibility  of
the office bearers in the light of the
observations herein above.
10

--- Page 49 ---
20. For the purposes of ascertaining as
to who was responsible and on whom the axe
must fall under sub-Section (5) of Section
75 of the 1960 Act, the parties shall be at
liberty to place additional documents before
the revisional authority.
21. We also make it clear that it shall
be open for the appellants to seek such
interim  protection  from  the  revisional
authority as they may be advised to seek
which shall be considered on its own merits.
22. With the aforesaid observations/
directions, this appeal stands disposed of.
23. Pending application(s), if any, shall
stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL ORIGINAL JURISDICTION
WRIT PETITION (CIVIL) NO.368/2025
ASHA  PETITIONER
                                VERSUS
STATE OF HARYANA RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. It  is  stated  that  the  petitioner(s)  has  received  the
compensation from the respondent – State of Haryana as ordered by
this Court. The submission made by the learned counsel for the

W.P. (C) No.368/2025:
1. Writ Petition is disposed of in terms of the singed order

--- Page 57 ---
W.P.(C) No.324/2020:
1. IA No.127085/2025 : The orders dated 12.11.2025, 13.11.2025
and 14.11.2025 passed by the State of Goa would indicate that the
amount of Rs.10 lakhs has been sanctioned in four cases. In fact,
this Court had clarified  on 20.01.2026  where the amounts having
been determined and paid prior to this Court’s judgment dated
20.10.2023, such claims need not be reopened. However, in case of
deaths having occurred prior to the judgment dated 20.10.2023, if
compensation has not been determined and paid as on the date of the
judgment, the concerned States or Municipal Authorities would be
required to pay a sum of Rs.30 lakhs in such of those claimants. It
was also clarified that in the event of compensation having not
been determined or paid in respect of deaths which had occurred
prior to the judgment dated 20.10.2023, the State would be liable
to pay compensation of Rs.30 lakhs to such of those claimants. Yet
by orders dated 12.11.2025, 13.11.2025 and 14.11.2025, the State of
Goa has only determined the compensation of Rs.10 lakhs which is
diametrically opposite to the judgment passed by this Court on
20.10.2023. Hence, the State of Goa to show-cause as to why the
judgment dated 20.10.2023 has not been complied and as to why
contempt proceedings should not be initiated against them.
Two weeks’ time is granted to file reply to the same. 
2. IA No.263173/2025 : Issue notice, returnable within one week
from today and also the perusal of the said application, it would
indicate  that  three  deaths  have  occurred  and  neither  the
compensation has been paid nor steps have been taken to prosecute
7

--- Page 58 ---
the concerned except making a show of FIR No.132/2025 having been
registered.
3. IA No.65476/2026 : The application is hereby allowed. Cause-
title shall be amended accordingly.

respondent No.27 – State of Uttar Pradesh to pay compensation of
Rs.30 lakhs as ordered by this court in judgment rendered in W.P.
(C) No.324/2020 on 20.10.2023 and to provide rehabilitation to the
families of deceased amongst other prayers.

is granted on payment of cost of Rs.25,000/- payable to Safai
Karamchari Commission within an outer limit of four weeks from

6. This  Court  by  judgment  dated  20.10.2023  amongst  other
directions had issued the following direction:
“96. In view of the above discussion, the following directions

(1) The Union should take appropriate measures and frame

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.            OF 2026

JISHI K.I.      APPELLANT(S)

CHANDRASEKHAR RAM & ORS.                     RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
Leave granted. 
2. The present appeals arise out of impugned orders
dated 08.11.2021 and 16.02.2022 passed by the High Court
of Kerala at Ernakulam in FAO(RO) No.23 of 2021 and in
I.A. No.1 of 2022 in FAO(RO) No.23 of 2021, respectively. 
3. By way of the impugned orders, the High Court, while
maintaining the order dated 08.01.2021 passed by the
Additional  District  Judge,  Irinjalakuda  (hereinafter
referred to as ‘first appellate court’), directed that
there would be an open remand for effecting a partition by
metes and bounds in respect of all of the plaint schedule
properties in accordance with the preliminary decree. 
1

--- Page 63 ---
4. Briefly stated, the facts of the case are that both
the  appellant  and  respondent  No.1  herein  are  the
successors-in-interest  of  late  Karuvathil  Ramankutty
(hereinafter  referred  to  as  the  ‘original  owner’).
Respondent No.1 herein had filed O.S. No.377 of 1999
before the Principal Sub Court, Irinjalakuda (hereinafter
referred to as ‘trial court’) , for partition and separate
possession of the plaint schedule properties belonging to
the  original  owner,  which  contained  five  separate
properties.  A  compromise  was  arrived  at  between  the
parties.  On  16.06.2003,  an  application  bearing  I.A.
No.1838/93 was filed in the aforesaid suit under Order
XXIII  Rule  3  of  the  Code  of  Civil  Procedure,  1908
(hereinafter referred to as “CPC”), which was signed by
all the parties, agreeing to effect a partition in terms
of the modalities specified therein.  The trial court
passed a preliminary decree dated 18.06.2003 in O.S.
No.377 of 1999, in terms of the compromise arrived at
between the parties.
5. The  original  defendant  No.1  (appellant’s  mother)
filed W.P.(C) No.22527 of 2007 before the High Court,
wherein, by judgment dated 23.07.2007, the Court clarified
2

--- Page 64 ---
the method of carrying out the partition of the plaint
schedule properties in terms of the compromise decree.
With respect to item No.3 of the plaint schedule property,
the Court observed that the said property had to be set
apart to the share of defendant No.1 and while assessing
its value, the house and improvements were not to be
valued,  but  only  the  land  wherein  the  building  was
situated and other areas and trees were to be valued for
the said purpose.  
6. Challenging the aforesaid judgment, a review petition
bearing RP No.40 of 2014 was filed by respondent No.1. The
High Court, by judgment dated 23.06.2014, disposed of the
said petition with the observation that the valuation of
the plaint schedule item No.3 would be assessed by the
Court in the final decree proceeding at the time of fixing
the owelty to be paid to the sharers. 
7. In the meanwhile, in I.A. No.3380 of 2003 filed by
respondent No.1 in O.S. No.377 of 1999 for passing a final
decree, the trial Court by judgment and order dated
16.09.2017,  passed  a  final  decree  in  terms  of  the
compromise arrived at between the parties and as per the
Advocate Commissioner’s report. Consequently, item No.3 of
3

--- Page 65 ---
the plaint schedule property was allotted exclusively to
the appellant, and as consideration, she was directed to
pay Rs.10,53,168/- to respondent No.1. 
8. Aggrieved by the valuation fixed by the trial court
with respect to plaint schedule item No.3, both appellant
and respondent No.1 filed separate appeals bearing A.S.
No.257 of 2017 and A.S. No.180 of 2019, respectively,
before the  first appellate court. The first appellate
court, by a common judgment dated 08.01.2021, disposed of
the aforesaid appeals by remitting the matter to the trial
court only for the purpose of recording the market value
of the property of plaint schedule property item No.3.
 
9. Being aggrieved, respondent No.1 filed an appeal
bearing FAO (RO) No.23 of 2021 before the High Court.  By
judgment dated 08.11.2021, the High Court directed that
there would be an open remand for effecting partition by
metes and bounds in respect of all the plaint schedule
properties in accordance with the preliminary decree.
Challenging the aforesaid judgment of the High Court, a
review application bearing I.A. No.1 of 2022 in FAO (RO)
No.23 of 2021 was preferred by the appellant herein. The
said review application was dismissed by the High Court
4

--- Page 66 ---
vide order dated 16.02.2022.
10. Being aggrieved by the order dated 08.11.2021 and
16.06.2022 passed by the High Court of Kerala at Ernakulam
in FAO (RO) No.23 of 2021 and in I.A. No.1 of 2022 in FAO
(RO) No.23 of 2021, the appellant has preferred these
appeals.
11. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant and
learned  senior  counsel  and  learned  counsel  for  the
respondents.
12. During the course of submissions, learned counsel for
the appellant drew our attention to the order dated
08.01.2021 by which the Court of the Additional District
Judge, Irinjalakuda, Thrissur-first appellate court had
remanded the matter to the trial court with certain
directions. The said remand was only for the purpose of
determining  the  market  value  of  the  plaint  schedule
property namely, item No.3 and certain directions were
also issued in that regard. But the said judgment dated
08.01.2021 was assailed by the respondent in FAO (RO)
No.23 of 2021. The High Court failed to notice that the
remand made by the first appellate court to the trial
court was only with regard to the valuation of the suit
5

--- Page 67 ---
schedule property, item No.3 and thus a closed remand. But
the High Court has remanded the matter as an open remand
for effecting partition by metes and bounds which was
beyond  what  was  the  initial  controversy  between  the
parties.  Learned  counsel  for  the  appellant  therefore
submitted that the impugned judgments may be set aside and
the judgment of the first appellate court may be restored
so that the trial court could determine the valuation
having regard to the directions issued therein. 
13. He further submitted that the proceedings before the
trial court arise out of a compromise decree passed in the
trial court and the respondents herein have not assailed
the said compromise decree and in fact have filed a final
decree proceeding for effectuating the compromise decree.
In the circumstances, the High Court could not have passed
such a direction for division of the property by metes and
bounds by directing an open remand. Hence, the impugned
judgment may be set aside and the judgment of the first
appellate court may be restored. 
14. Per  contra,  learned  counsel  for  the  respondents
contended that although there is no challenge to the
compromise decree nevertheless the High Court thought it
6

--- Page 68 ---
fit in the interest of justice to remand the matter for
the purpose of effecting partition by metes and bounds.
The same has been done at the instance of the respondent
herein in the appeal filed against the judgment passed by
the first appellate court. There is no error in the
impugned judgment and hence, the appeal may be dismissed.
15. We have taken note of the submissions made at the
bar. 
16. Admittedly, there was a compromise decree passed
between the parties which has attained finality inasmuch
as there has been no challenge to the same. The final
decree proceeding was in fact initiated by the respondent
herein for giving effect to the compromise decree. In the
controversy, which arose with regard to the valuation of
the suit item No.3, the matter traveled from the trial
court to the first appellate court which had remanded the
same  to  the  trial  court  for  the  purpose  of  re-
determination of the market value of suit item No.3.
However, we find that the respondent has sought to go
behind the compromise by filing an appeal before the High
Court which has in fact also not passed the judgment in
accordance with what was necessary to be done in the final
7

--- Page 69 ---
decree proceedings, namely determining the valuation of
suit item No.3 as much water had flown pursuant to the
compromise decree. 
17. In the circumstances, we set aside the impugned
judgment of the High Court and restore the judgment of the
first appellate court. The matter shall now stand remanded
to the trial court for complying with the directions of
the first appellate court. 
18. The trial court shall endeavour to dispose of the
final decree proceeding as expeditiously as possible.
19. These appeals are allowed in the aforesaid terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

THE CHAIRMAN AND MANAGING DIRECTOR, STATE

APPELLANT(S)
                              VERSUS
D. VIJAYKUMAR & ORS. RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) No.10233/2023]
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) No. 10234/2023]
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) Nos. 6363-6424/2023]
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) No. 10231/2023]
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) Nos. 10235-10236/2023]
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) Nos. 10239-10325/2023]
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) Nos. 10327-10328/2023]
CIVIL APPEAL NOS.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) Nos. 22770-22856/2025]
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) No.         OF 2026]
[Diary No(s). 42231/2026]
1

--- Page 73 ---
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
[SLP(C) No.         OF 2026]
[Diary No(s). 42219/2026]
O R D E R
1. Delay condoned.
2. Leave granted.
3. The issue that arises for consideration in these
cases  is  whether  the  respondent  –  landowners  are
entitled to be paid compensation for their acquired land
in  accordance  with  provision  of  the  Right  to  Fair
Compensation  and  Transparency  in  Land  Acquisition,
Rehabilitation and Resettlement Act, 2013 (in short,
‘2013 Act’) with cut-off date of 01.01.2014 or as per
the rate determined under the Tamil Nadu Acquisition of
Land for Industrial Purposes Act, 1997 (in short, ‘1997
Act’).
4. The  State  of  Tamil  Nadu  accorded  administrative
approval to acquire 970 acres of land in favour of the
State Industrial Corporation on 06.01.2009. Thereafter,
a notification under Section 3(2) of the 1997 Act was
issued on 27.10.2009. This was followed by a public
notice  in  Form  ‘B’  on  the  same  date.  The  State
Government, after waiting for two years, published a
notification in the Government Gazette on 13.12.2011.
However, no award was passed. Meanwhile, writ petitions
2

--- Page 74 ---
were filed challenging certain provisions of the rules
framed by the State Government under the 1997 Act. We
are informed that interim protection was granted by the
High Court in those writ petitions on different dates
during the year 2012 to 2013. 
5. Section 7 of the 1997 Act deals with “determination
and payment of amount”. Sub-section (1) provides that
where any land is acquired by the State Government under
this Act, compensation for such land shall be determined
in accordance with the provisions of this section. Sub-
section (6) of Section 7 has a material bearing, and it
reads as follows:
“7(6) In determining the amount, the Collector
shall be guided by the provisions contained in
sections  23  and  24  and  other  relevant
provisions of the of the Land Acquisition Act,
1894 subject to modifications that-
(a) in the said section 23, the references to
the date of publication of the notification
under section 4, sub-section (1) and the time
of publication of the declaration under section
6  of  the  said  Act  shall  be  construed  as
reference to the date of publication of notice
under sub-section (20 and (1) respectively of
section 3 of this Act; and
(b) in the said section 24, the references to
the date of publication of notification under
section 4, sub-section (1) and the date of
publication of the declaration under section 6
of  the  said  Act  shall  be  construed  as
references to the date of publication of notice
under sub-section (2) and (1) respectively of
section 3 of this Act.”
6. It may also be explained at this stage that barring
Section 7, the 1997 Act does not describe any mechanism
3

--- Page 75 ---
for  acquisition  of  land.  It  is  obvious  that  the
acquisition process, as mandated by Section 7(6) of the
1997 Act, was required to be completed in accordance
with the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act, 1894
(in short, ‘1894 Act’). Even otherwise, the acquisition
proceeding was to be concluded and the award made within
a reasonable time.
7. The  1894  Act  came  to  be  repealed  with  the
enforcement of the 2013 Act with effect from 01.01.2014.
Section 24 of the 2013 Act too has some relevance, and
it reads as follows:
“24. Land acquisition process under Act No. 1 of
1894 shall be deemed to have lapsed in certain
cases.–(1) Notwithstanding anything contained in
this  Act,  in  any  case  of  land  acquisition
proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition
Act, 1894,—
(a) where no award under section 11 of the said
Land Acquisition Act has been made, then, all
provisions  of  this  Act  relating  to  the
determination of compensation shall apply; or
(b) where an award under said section 11 has
been made, then such proceedings shall continue
under  the  provisions  of  the  said  Land
Acquisition Act, as if the said Act has not been
repealed.
(2) Notwithstanding anything contained in sub-
section  (1),  in  case  of  land  acquisition
proceedings initiated under the Land Acquisition
Act, 1894 (1 of 1894),where an award under the
said section 11 has been made five years or more
prior to the commencement of this Act but the
physical possession of the land has not been
taken or the compensation has not been paid the
said proceedings shall be deemed to have lapsed
and  the  appropriate  Government,  if  it  so
chooses, shall initiate the proceedings of such
land acquisition afresh in accordance with the
provisions of this Act:
4

--- Page 76 ---
Provided that where an award has been made and
compensation in respect of a majority of land
holdings has not been deposited in the account
of the beneficiaries, then, all beneficiaries
specified in the notification for acquisition
under section 4 of the said Land Acquisition
Act,  shall  be  entitled  to  compensation  in
accordance with the provisions of this Act.”
[Emphasis Supplied]
8. In the pending writ petitions, the question that
arose for consideration was whether, in light of the new
statutory regime which came into force w.e.f 01.01.2014,
the  respondent-landowners  were  entitled  to  be  paid
compensation for the acquired land in accordance with
the provisions of the 2013 Act, with cut-off date of
01.01.2014 or the State of Tamil Nadu was competent to
pass an award under the old regime.
9. It is an admitted fact that despite notification
under Section 3(2) of the 1997 Act having been made in
2009, no award could be passed before 01.01.2014. It is
true that interim orders came to be passed sometime in
2012-2013,  but  considerable  time  had  lapsed  between
issuance of notification under Section 3 of the 1997 Act
and such interim orders and no award had been made in
the meantime. It is no longer res integra that after the
2013  Act  came  into  force,  the  pending  acquisition
processes, where an award was yet to be passed, were
required to be completed under Section 24(1)(a) of the
2013 Act and the award was required to be passed in such
cases based on the market value of the land as on
5

--- Page 77 ---
01.01.2014. This is precisely what the High Court has
done in the instant case.
10. We may hasten to add that in view of Section 7(6) of
the  1997  Act  (State  Act),  the  expression  ‘Land
Acquisition Act, 1894’ shall be deemed to have been
substituted  by  the  ‘Right  to  Fair  Compensation  and
Transparency  in  Land  Acquisition,  Rehabilitation  and
Resettlement Act, 2013’ as the emphasis made by State
Legislation is on the ‘Central Act’. There is no quarrel
that at the time the award came to be passed, the
Central Act in force governing the acquisition of land
was the 2013 Act. 
11. In this view of the matter, we find that the High
Court has not committed any error in holding that the
respondent-landowners  are  entitled  to  be  paid
compensation in accordance with the provisions of the
2013 Act based on the market value to be determined as
on 01.01.2014. 
12. For  the  reasons  aforesaid,  the  appeals  are
dismissed. The appellants are directed to proceed in
accordance with law. 
13. However, if the State of Tamil Nadu finds that the
acquisition will not be viable in public interest on
account of the alleged excessive payment of compensation
under the 2013 Act, they shall be at liberty to release
6

--- Page 78 ---
the subject land from acquisition and restore the same
to  the  landowners  free  from  all  encumbrances.  An
appropriate  decision  in  this  regard  shall  be  taken
within eight weeks.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP (C) NO.25416 OF 2023)
GEETA BAI       APPELLANT(S) 
VERSUS
KANCHANLAL & ANR.            RESPONDENT(S)
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL  NO.         OF 2026
Arising out of SLP (C) NO.27816 OF 2023)
O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. These appeals arise out of a common judgment and order
dated 29.08.2023 passed by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at
Indore in First Appeal Nos.487 of 2010 and 202 of 2003. 
3. For  the  sake  of  convenience,  the  parties  shall
hereinafter be referred to by their respective names.  
4. Briefly  stated,  the  facts  of  the  case  are  that
agricultural  land  bearing  Sy  No.1349/2  admeasuring  1.383
hectares situated at village Runji, Gautampura (hereinafter
1

--- Page 83 ---
referred to as ‘suit schedule property’) was recorded in the
name of one Hiralal. Following the demise of Hiralal, the suit
schedule  property  was  mutated  in  favour  of  his  wife,
Reshambai.  However,  the  name  of  the  appellant  herein,
Geetabai, who is the daughter of Hiralal, was not included in
the  revenue  records.  Being  aggrieved,  Geetabai  initiated
revenue proceedings, and after several rounds of litigation,
her name was directed to be included in the revenue records as
a co-sharer in the suit schedule property.
 
5. Meanwhile, a purported agreement to sell dated 14.06.1994
was executed by Reshambai (mother of Geetabai) in favour of
the respondent herein, Kanchanlal, with respect to the suit
schedule  property.  After  the  death  of  Reshambai,  the
subsequent purchaser, Kanchanlal, submitted an application for
mutation on the basis of the purported agreement to sell dated
14.06.1994,  which  came  to  be  allowed  by  order  dated
29.05.1997. Thereafter, it is alleged that he forcefully took
possession of the suit-schedule property. 
6. Being aggrieved, Geeta Bai filed Civil Suit No.3A of 2002
(old No.11A of 1998) before the Civil Judge Class 2, Depalpur,
Indore, seeking declaration, possession and cancellation of
mutation effected before the revenue authorities in favour of
Kanchanlal, based on the alleged agreement dated 14.06.1994.
Parallelly, Kanchanlal also filed Civil Suit No.63A of 2000
2

--- Page 84 ---
before the Additional District Judge, Indore, seeking specific
performance of the agreement to sell dated 14.06.1994 as well
as permanent injunction with an alternative prayer for refund
of the consideration paid pursuant to the execution of the
aforesaid agreement. 
7. The 11 th Additional District Judge, Indore (hereinafter
referred to as the‘trial court’) by common judgment dated
02.01.2003, decreed the suit for declaration in favour of
Geeta Bai and partly decreed the suit for specific performance
filed by Kanchanlal to the extent of directing payment of
Rs.42,750/- in his favour towards damages. 
8. Being aggrieved by the common judgment passed by the
trial court in Civil Suit No.63A of 2000 and Civil Suit No.3A
of 2002 (old No.11A of 1998), Kanchanlal preferred separate
first appeals bearing First Appeal No.202 of 2003 and First
Appeal No.487 of 2010, respectively, before the High Court of
Madhya Pradesh at Indore.
9. By way of the common impugned judgment and order dated
29.08.2023, the High Court observed that the trial court,
while considering the suit for specific performance filed by
Kanchanlal, had concluded that the said suit was barred by
limitation, being filed after more than four years from the
date of execution of the agreement and further the agreement
3

--- Page 85 ---
entered into between Kanchanlal and Reshambai (Geeta Bai’s
mother) being vague could not have been made binding on her
daughter, Geeta Bai. In view of the aforesaid findings made by
the trial court, the High Court held that it was open to the
trial court to then partly allow the said suit to the extent
of awarding damages of Rs.42,750/- in favour of Kanchanlal. 
10. With respect to the suit for declaration filed by Geeta
Bai, the High Court held that the evidence adduced by Geeta
Bai through her son, Gopal (power of attorney holder) was
liable to be discarded in view of the settled law that a power
of attorney holder cannot depose on behalf of the principal
for acts, transactions or dealings of the principal of which
the principal alone has knowledge. Thus, it was held that the
suit for declaration filed by Geeta Bai would fail. 
11. Based on the aforesaid findings, the High Court allowed
First Appeal No.487 of 2010 arising out of Civil Suit No.3A of
2002, and consequently, the judgment and decree passed in
favour of Geeta Bai, was set aside. Similarly, First Appeal
No.202 of 2003 arising out of Civil Suit No.63A of 2002 was
dismissed, and the decree of damages passed in favour of
Kanchanlal was set aside. 
12. Being aggrieved by the common judgment passed in the said
appeals, the parties have preferred their respective appeals
4

--- Page 86 ---
before this Court.
13. We have heard learned counsel for the appellant/Geeta Bai
and learned counsel for respondent(s)/ Kanchanlal/appellant in
the connected matter and perused the material on record.
14. During the course of submissions, it was brought to our
notice that the possession of the suit scheduled property
which was in fact with the plaintiff, who had filed a suit
seeking the relief of specific performance which has now been
transferred to the plaintiff, who has sought the relief of
declaration of title and possession in her suit.
15. Learned counsel for the respective parties submitted that
there is no dispute about the said fact. It was also submitted
that if agreement to sell dated 14.06.1994 is accepted, then a
sum Rs.85,000/- was paid by the plaintiff/Kanchanlal, who
filed the suit, to Resham Bai W/o Hiral Lal Joshi. Smt. Geeta
Bai is their daughter, who is presently in possession of the
suit scheduled property. 
16. Having regard to the developments which have taken place
in the matter and the fact that the agreement itself is dated
14.06.1994,  learned  counsel  for  the  respective  parties
submitted that if a quietus could be given to this litigation
in an amicable way, the parties may accept the same.
5

--- Page 87 ---
17. One of the suggestions made was whether having regard to
agreement to sell dated  14.06.1994  under which a sum of
Rs.85,000/- is said to have been paid by Kanchanlal to Resham
Bai, mother of Geeta Bai, the said amount could be returned
with reasonable interest from   14.06.1994 till the date of
realisation  so  that  the  suit  filed  seeking  specific
performance of the agreement could be disposed of by way of an
alternative  relief  and  consequently,  the  suit  filed  for
seeking declaration of title and possession could also be
decreed and disposed.
18. We have considered the submissions made at the Bar.
19. We find that having regard to the long litigation between
the parties and agreement to sell dated 14.06.1994, the ends
of justice would be served in the instant cases if the
appellant/Smt. Geeta Bai is permitted to retain the possession
of  the  suit  scheduled  property  and  the  suit  filed  by
Kanchanlal for specific performance of the agreement to sell
dated  14.06.1994  could  be  disposed  of  by  granting  the
alternative relief.  The alternative relief would be payment
of Rs.85,000/- with interest @ 10% per annum from 14.06.1994
till realisation to Kanchanlal. The said payment shall be made
within a period of two months from today.
20. It  is  needless  to  observe  that  in  case  the  said
6

--- Page 88 ---
settlement is not acted upon, liberty is reserved to the
respondent(s)/Kanchanlal to move this Court by making an
appropriate application. 
21. Consequently, the suit filed for specific performance of
the agreement to sell dated 14.06.1994 is disposed of in the
aforesaid terms. 
22. The  suit  filed  for  declaration  of  title  and  for
possession also stands decreed.  The appellant/Geeta Bai is
declared to be the owner in possession of the suit scheduled
property.
23. The Appeals are disposed of in the aforesaid terms. 
No costs.
Pending application (s) shall stand disposed of.

Civil Appeal  No(s).  9768/2026
@ Diary No. 18254/2026
EMPLOYEES PROVIDENT FUND ORGANISATION              Appellant(s)
                             
VERSUS
RACHNA JHUNJHUNWALA & ANR.                      Respondent(s)
O R D E R
 
1. Refiling delay condoned.
2. Aggrieved by exclusion of unadjudicated
claims  of  the  appellant  qua interest  and
damages payable under Section 7Q and Section
14B, respectively, of the Employees’ Provident
Funds and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1952
(for short,  the 1952  Act) in  the approved
resolution plan, the appellant filed an appeal
before  the  National  Company  Law  Appellate
Tribunal  (NCLAT)  against  the  order  of  the
Adjudicating Authority approving such plan. The
1

--- Page 92 ---
said appeal stood dismissed by the impugned
order.
3. The Corporate Debtor (CD) was admitted
into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process
(CIRP) vide order of the Adjudicating Authority
dated  01.05.2023.  Pursuant  to  public
announcement  inviting  claims,  the  Appellant
submitted a claim of Rs.22,49,956/- comprising
provident fund (PF) dues including interest and
damages payable under Sections 7Q and 14B of
the 1952 Act. During CIRP, the Committee of
Creditors (COC) with 100% voting share approved
the  resolution  plan  and  submitted  it  for
approval of the Adjudicating Authority. The
Adjudicating Authority approved it  vide order
dated 17.05.2024.
4. Under the Resolution Plan, Rs.73,120/-
was proposed to be paid towards PF dues of the
CD as against the claim of Rs.22,49,956/-.
Notably, the claim of Rs.22,49,956 included (a)
Rs.73,120/- towards PF dues under Section 7A;
(b)  Rs.9,32,805/-  towards  interest  leviable
under  Section  7Q;  and  (c)  Rs.12,44,031/-
towards damages under Section 14B.
2

--- Page 93 ---
5. The argument on behalf of the Appellant was
that PF dues are excluded from liquidation
estate  under  Section  36(4)(a)(iii)  of  the
Insolvency  and  Bankruptcy  Code,  2016  (for
short, IBC) and, therefore, could not have been
subjected to reduction, or haircut, under the
resolution plan.
6. Per contra, in support of the resolution
plan,  the  argument  was  that  prior  to
commencement of CIRP, the appellant had not
passed any order of determination under either
Section 7A or Section 14B of the 1952 Act, and
therefore, those dues had not crystallized. In
so far as employer’s (CD’s) PF contribution is
concerned, the same was provided for in the
resolution  plan.  It  was  submitted  that
resolution plan was passed by COC with 100%
voting share  and has  been approved  by the
Adjudicating Authority; therefore, in absence
of  any  statutory  violations,  the  plan  so
approved is not liable to be interfered with.
7. The  NCLAT  found  that  proceedings
relating to interest and damages claimed under
the  1952  Act  were  initiated  on  10.05.2023
3

--- Page 94 ---
whereas  CIRP  had  commenced  on  01.05.2023;
therefore,  the  claim  under  the  heads  of
interest and damages was neither crystallized
nor could be adjudicated upon in view of the
moratorium. Thus, the protection of Section
36(4)(a)(iii) of IBC to those claims was not
available. Based on that reasoning, the NCLAT
declined to interfere with the approval of the
resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority.
8. We have heard learned counsel for the
appellant. He pressed the same arguments as
were urged on behalf of the appellant before
the NCLAT.
9. In Tata Steel Ltd. versus Varsha & Anr.,
2026 SCC  OnLine SC  1349 ,  this Court  while
directing quashing of arbitral proceedings qua
claims not provided for in the resolution plan
observed as under:
“55. This court is further of the view
that no resolution plan can succeed if
uncertain  or  unquantified  claims  are
permitted to linger and resurface against
the successful resolution applicant years
after approval. Such a situation would be
akin to a hydra headed recurrence and is
antithetical  to  the  ‘clean  slate’
principle.”
4

--- Page 95 ---
10. The rationale behind the above view is
spelt out in Essar Steel (India) Ltd. Committee
of Creditors v. Satish Kumar Gupta, (2020) 8
SCC 531, where this Court held:
“107. … A successful resolution applicant
cannot suddenly be faced with undecided
claims after the resolution plan submitted
by him has been accepted as this would
amount to a hydra head popping up which
would  throw  into  uncertainty  amounts
payable  by  a  prospective  resolution
applicant who would successfully take over
the business of the corporate debtor. All
claims must be submitted to and decided by
the  resolution  professional  so  that  a
prospective  resolution  applicant  knows
exactly what has to be paid in order that
it may then take over and run the business
of the corporate debtor.” 
11. In our view, though PF dues are excluded from
the liquidation estate under Section 36(4)(iii)
of IBC, liability of CD towards interest and
damages payable under Section 7Q and 14B of the
1952 Act, if not determined and finalized before
CIRP commencement, would fall in the category of
a contingent liability. To assuage the concern of
all stakeholders, the COC, in its commercial
wisdom, may provide for a lump sum amount to meet
contingent  liabilities  arising  from
uncrystallized claims. However, if the COC, in
its commercial wisdom, has not provided for such
5

--- Page 96 ---
contingent liabilities in the resolution plan,
its  decision  cannot  be  faulted  because  the
underlying object of CIRP is to adhere to fixed
timelines.  If  the  prospective  resolution
applicant is kept guessing as to what he would
have to pay to take over and run the business of
the  CD,  it  may  not  enter  the  fray  thereby
defeating the underlying object of IBC. Besides,
approval of a resolution plan duly approved by
the COC  can be  declined by  the Adjudicating
Authority on limited grounds, inter alia, that it
does not fulfill the mandate of sub-section (2)
of Section 30 of IBC. 
12. Here the resolution plan provides for payment
of PF dues even though it does not provide for
uncrystallized claims of interest and damages
regarding which proceedings were not initiated by
the CIRP commencement date. Therefore, in our
view,  there  is  no  blatant  violation  of  the
statutory mandate of IBC.
13. For all the reasons above, we do not find any
justification  to  interfere  with  the  impugned
order which affirms the order of the Adjudicating
Authority  approving  the  resolution  plan.  The
6

--- Page 97 ---
appeal  is,  accordingly,  dismissed.  Pending
application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.
………………………………………..J
[MANOJ MISRA]
…………………………………………..J

New Delhi;
July 28, 2026

CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.        OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(C) NO.25281 OF 2026)
MANIPAL TECHNOLOGIES LIMITED & ANOTHER        APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS

 O R D E R
Leave granted.
2. We have heard learned senior counsel, Mr. C. Aryama
Sundaram for the appellants and learned counsel, Mr. Kush
Sharma for respondent No.1-Bank. 
3. On perusal of the impugned order passed by the
Division Bench of the High Court, we find that the writ
appeal was against the order dated 08.06.2026 passed by
the learned Single Judge in Writ Petition No.16741/2026
declining to grant interim relief. The Division Bench of
the High Court in the impugned order in Writ Appeal
No.1602/2026 at paragraph ‘1’ as well as paragraph ‘47’
notes that there was no ground to interfere with the
impugned order passed by the learned Single Judge which is
1

--- Page 107 ---
dated 08.06.2026. Consequently, our understanding of the
impugned order is that the Division Bench of the High
Court also refused to grant an interim order in the
matter. 
4. The Writ Petition No.16741/2026 was ordered to be
listed on 23.07.2026 by the learned Single Judge.
5. Learned senior counsel for the appellants submitted
that in view of the detailed impugned order of the
Division Bench, it appears that there is no substance as
such in the writ petition inasmuch as it is implied that
the  writ  petition  itself  has  been  dismissed  by  the
Division  Bench  of  the  High  Court.  Therefore  it  was
submitted that having regard to the fact that what was
challenged by the appellants before the Division Bench of
the High Court in the writ appeal was an order declining
to grant interim relief and the writ petition is still at
large to be argued on merits, appropriate orders may be
made with regard to the impugned order so that the
appellants’ right to make submissions on merits in the
writ petition is saved and reserved.
2

--- Page 108 ---
6. In response to this submission, learned counsel for
the  first  respondent-Bank  which  is  the  contesting
respondent brought to our notice the fact that in view of
there being no interim order as against the Bank, it has
proceeded to issue the work order/award the tender to
respondent Nos.2 and 3 and they are presently on the verge
of commencing their work in terms of the said tender. He
also submitted that the Division Bench of the High Court
was justified in considering the matter on merits, having
regard to the fact that arguments were advanced on the
merits  of  the  case.  Learned  counsel  for  the  first
respondent-Bank therefore submitted that there is no merit
in this appeal.
7. We have considered the arguments advanced at the bar
in light of the fact that Writ Petition No.16741/2026 is
still pending consideration before the learned Single
Judge of the High Court. The writ petition was to be heard
on 23.07.2026. 
8. Writ Appeal No.1602/2026 was an appeal filed by the
appellants herein being aggrieved by not being granted an
interim relief in the aforesaid writ petition.
3

--- Page 109 ---
9. In  view  of  the  fact  that  the  High  Court  has
considered the controversy in light of the aforesaid
impugned order passed by the learned Single Judge, we
dispose of this appeal by observing that the appellants
herein  are  at  liberty  to  make  submissions  in  W.P.
No.16741/2026 on the merits. The impugned order passed by
the Division Bench shall be construed to be an order
giving reasons only for declining to grant interim relief.
10. In view of the above, we observe that all contentions
on both sides on the merits of the writ petition are left
open to be argued in the writ petition. This appeal is
disposed of in the aforesaid terms.
11. Since the matter pertains to grant of tender, the
learned  Single  Judge  is  requested  to  hear  the  writ
petition as expeditiously as possible and dispose of the
same within a period of two months from the date on which
the matter is listed next before the learned Single Judge.
12. The parties are at liberty to move the learned Single
Judge for seeking listing of the matter as it was already
slated to be listed on 23.07.2026. 
4

--- Page 110 ---
13. Since we have not passed any adverse order as against
respondent Nos.2 and 3 in this appeal, we have not issued
notices to them. We also observe that tenders awarded to
respondent Nos.2 and 3 would be subject to the result of
the writ petition.
14. This appeal is disposed of in the aforesaid terms
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

ITEM NO.53               COURT NO.3               SECTION IV-A
               S U P R E M E  C O U R T  O F  I N D I A
                       RECORD OF PROCEEDINGS
Petition for Special Leave to Appeal (C)  No(s).  25281/2026
[Arising out of impugned final judgment and order dated  16-

          UPON hearing the counsel the Court made the following
                             O R D E R
1. Heard learned counsel for the parties.

--- Page 114 ---
2
2. The present petitions call in question the correctness of
judgment and final order(s) dated 06-12-2019 passed by the
High Court of Jharkhand at Ranchi in Criminal Revision Nos.
47/2016 & 57/2016.
3. The petitioner and respondent no.2 are estranged couple.
Respondent no.2 claims that he has an  ex-parte decree of
divorce in his favour.
4. Be that as it may, the present proceedings arise out of a
maintenance  claim  filed  by  the  petitioner  herein.  The
concerned Trial Court had, originally on 15.01.2007, ordered
the  respondent  no.2  to  pay  a  maintenance  allowance  of
Rs.5,000/- per month to the petitioner herein and another
Rs.2,000/- per month to minor daughter Shreya with effect from
the date of filing of the case i.e. 20.12.2005. Thereafter, by
an order of 17.10.2015, the concerned Court modified the
amount  to  that  of  Rs.6,000/-  per  month  in  all  for  the
petitioner herself and her daughter. The order of 17.10.2015
was  to  operate  from  the  date  of  the  order  as  per  the
directions of the Principal Judge, Family Court, Hazaribagh.
5. Both parties carried the matter to the High Court. The
High Court maintained the order of the Trial Court. Insofar as
the date of operation is concerned that would mean that the
maintenance as ordered on 17.10.2015, was to operate from the
said date.
6. The respondent no.2 has accepted the said order of the
High Court dated 06.12.2019. 
7. The petitioner, aggrieved by the denial of maintenance

--- Page 115 ---
3
from the date of application, is before us.
8. When  the  matter  came  up  on  17.02.2026,  this  Court
directed the respondent no.2 to pay 50% of the arrears i.e.
Rs.18,00,000/- within a period of four weeks. Thereafter, the
matter came up on 28.04.2026, when this Court noticing that
none appeared for respondent no.2 and that the amount also had
not  been  paid,  issued  non-bailable  warrants  against  the
respondent no.2 and directed production of respondent no.2
before this Court on 15.07.2026. 
9. On 15.07.2026, the matter could not be taken up, since
one of the Hon’ble Judge had to recuse. That is how the matter
is before us today.
10. Today, the respondent no.2 in pursuance of the non-
bailable warrants, has been produced before us by Mr.Satendra
Ram, Sub-Inspector of Police, Lalpania O.P./Lalpania P.S.,
Thana Mahuatad/Mahuatand, District Bokaro, Jharkhand, pursuant
to the remand order dated 27.07.2026 passed by the Judicial
Magistrate First Class, Bermo at Tenughat, Jharkhand. That
remand order is taken on record.
11. Mr.  Dushyant  Parashar,  learned  counsel  appears  for
respondent no.2. We have enquired from respondent no.2 as to
why the amount as directed, has not been paid. Respondent no.2
states that he does not have the means to pay any amount.
12. We cannot let the matter rest here.
13. Ms.  Shashi  Kiran,  learned  Senior  Counsel  for  the
petitioner submits that respondent no.2 is working at Tenughat
Vidyut Nigam Limited(for short, ‘TVNL’), which is situated at

2 SLP(C) No. 7735/2021
against the order dated 29.03.2021 passed in O.S.A.

2. The O.S.A. was filed with a delay of 1808
days,  challenging  the  order  dated  02.06.2015,
passed in Company Application No. 1409 of 2014
under Company Petition No. 66 of 1997.
3. Through the impugned order, the prayer for
condonation of delay has been rejected. Hence, the
special leave petition.
4. The above is both the introduction and also
concludes the present special leave petition for
the request for condonation was rejected for valid
reasons.  But  the  crux  of  the  matter  lies  in
between.
5. Respondent No.1 is the successful purchaser
of the properties of M/s. Gangavathi Sugar Mills
Limited (Company under Liquidation) in C.P. No. 66
of 1997. In the first instance, before obtaining a
regular transfer deed in its favour, the first
respondent filed an application to secure vacant
possession of all the properties, including the
property  stated  to  be  in  the  petitioner’s
possession before us. By order dated 02.06.2015,
the application in C.A. No. 1409 of 2014 in C.P.
No. 66 of 1997 was disposed of, and the operative

--- Page 121 ---
3 SLP(C) No. 7735/2021
portion reads thus:
“3. However, since the very conveyance
of title in favour of the applicant is
pending consideration before the Division
Bench which is dealing with the appeal
preferred against the order passed by this
Court confirming the sale in favour of the
applicant, the applicant would necessarily
have to await the decision in that appeal.
Therefore, if the school is indeed being
run by the third respondent, it would not
be fair to direct ejectment of the third
respondent forthwith. The same could be
postponed  till  such  time  the  applicant
obtains  a  confirmed  order  of  sale  in
respect of the land and deed of conveyance
in  favour  of  the  applicant.  The  third
respondent is permitted to carry on its
activity till such time title is conferred
on the applicant in due course. In the
event of such order being passed during the
currency of an academic year, it is also
directed that the third respondent may be
permitted to carry on its activity till the
end of that academic year and thereafter,
the third respondent shall quit and deliver
vacant possession.
Ordered accordingly.”
6. The first respondent, vide sale deed dated
05.05.2018, has become the owner after complying

--- Page 122 ---
4 SLP(C) No. 7735/2021
with all the obligations in the purchase of the

“WHEREFORE,  the  applicant  respectfully

7. The prayer has a chequered history. For at

5 SLP(C) No. 7735/2021

10. The submissions are taken note of. P rima
facie, we are of the view that the prayer in the

Secondly,  the  substantive  prayer  of  the  first

dispose of the Company Application No. 293 of 2018
expeditiously.

disposed of.

O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The appellant, who is the wife
of the detenue, has preferred the
present appeal, being aggrieved
by  the  dismissal  of  the  writ
petition  by  the  High  Court,
seeking  setting  aside  of  the
detention  order  passed  against
the detenue. 
3.  Learned  counsel  for  the
SLP (CRL) NO.6765/2026 1/4

--- Page 138 ---
appellant raised only one issue,
as recorded by this Court while
issuing notice, that there is a
clear  non-application  of  mind
with respect to the antecedents
of  the  appellant.  While  the
appellant’s  conviction  was
modified  to  the  offence
punishable  under  Part  II  of
Section 304 of the Indian Penal
Code, 1860 (‘IPC’), it was noted
that  he  was  convicted  under
Section 302 of the IPC.
4.  While  not  disputing  the
aforesaid error, learned counsel
for the State submitted that this
should not enure to the benefit
of the appellant. 
5. This is a case of clear non-
application of mind. The facts
have been wrongly recorded, and
SLP (CRL) NO.6765/2026 2/4

--- Page 139 ---
the detaining authority, if not
for the same, perhaps would not
have passed the detention order.
6. Considering the above, we are
inclined to set aside the order
of detention as well as the order
of the High Court.
7.  Accordingly,  the  impugned
order and the order of detention
are set aside and the appellant
shall  be  released  forthwith
unless  required  in  any  other
case.
8. The Appeal stands allowed.
9.  Pending  application(s),  if
any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
@ SLP (CRL.) NO.7417/2026
ABIMANYU     APPELLANT
                        VERSUS
STATE OF UTTAR PRADESH         RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. The  case  of  the  prosecution  based on  FIR
No.615/2024 came to be registered against appellant for
the offences punishable under Sections 352, 115(2) and
308(5) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
4. It is the case of the prosecution that an incident
occurred  on  07.11.2024  involving  assault  on  the
complainant resulting in injuries being sustained by him.
Undisputedly,  the  FIR  was  registered  against  three
1

--- Page 144 ---
unknown  persons  and  it  is  during  the  course  of  the
investigation, the name of the appellant surfaced, namely,
on  the  basis  of  statements  of  the  co-accused  persons
recorded  by  the  Investigating  Agency.  Thus,  the
prosecution  case  rests on  material  gathered  post
registration of the FIR and material collected during the
investigation. In this background, while issuing notice on
this petition vide order dated 24.04.2026, we had granted
interim protection to the appellant subject to cooperating
with  the  investigation.  Subsequently,  learned  counsel
appearing for the State, who appeared before this Court,
made a statement that appellant is not appearing, which
was  rebutted  by  the  learned  counsel  for  the  appellant
contending  that  when  appellant  had  contacted  the
Investigating  Officer,  he  had  been  informed  by  the
Investigating  Officer  that  as  and  when  his  presence  is
required,  he  would  be  summoned  and  as  such  it  was
contended  that  appellant  never  abstained  himself  from
appearing  before  the  Investigating  Officer.  It  is  in  this
background,  we  directed  the  appellant  –  accused  to
2

--- Page 145 ---
appear before the Investigating Officer on 18.07.2026 at
11:00 a.m. vide our order dated 17.07.2026. The learned
counsel appearing for the State would fairly submit that
pursuant to the said order, the appellant has appeared
before  the  Investigating  Officer.  However,  he  would
contend that on account of the gravity of the offence, the
appellant being a personnel from a discipline force ought
not  to  have  indulged  in  such  an  act  and  as  such  the
discretionary relief should not be granted. 
5. At the cost of the repetition, we notice that initially
the name of the appellant did not surface in the FIR and it
is  only  based  on  the  co-accused’s  statement,  the
appellant has been arraigned as an accused. That apart,
appellant has  appeared  before  the  Investigating  Officer
and cooperated with the investigation. Hence, we are of
the considered view that his custodial interrogation is not
warranted.  Hence,  we  allow  this  appeal  and  direct  the
appellant  to  be  released  on  anticipatory  bail  by  the
Investigating Officer on such terms and conditions as he
deems fit to impose including the condition of directing
3

--- Page 146 ---
the appellant to appear once in a week, namely, on every
Thursday between 11:00 A.M. to 02:00 P .M. till filing of the
chargesheet, if any against the appellant and shall also
appear before the trial court on all dates of hearing except
when exempted.
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed
of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
(Criminal Appeal No.     /2026)
(Arising out of SLP (Crl) No.     /2026)
(SLP(Crl) Diary No(s). 36403/2026)
NISHA                                Appellant(s)
VERSUS
STATE NCT OF DELHI                   Respondent(s)
O R D E R
1.  Heard.
2.  Delay condoned.
3. Leave granted.
4. Appellant has been named as an accused in FIR No.
693/2024 registered at Police Station Pandya Nagar, East
Delhi,  Delhi  on  16.12.2024  for  the  offence  punishable
under  Section  103(1),  115(2),  109(1)  and  3(5)  of  the
Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (“for short BNS”) and she is
seeking for being enlarged on regular bail . On completion
of the investigation, chargesheet has been filed and the
case is at the stage of framing of the charge. 
   
  SLP(Crl) Diary No(s). 36403/2026                                                                            1   

--- Page 156 ---
5. The appellant having approached the trial Court and
the  High  Court  for  grant  of  bail  has  suffered  order  of
rejection, as such she is before this Court. Both the Courts
have taken note of the statement of the complainant to
reject the  prayer and have  arrived at a conclusion that
there is possibility of public witnesses being threatened or
influenced and same cannot be ruled out to.
6.  The chargesheet material having been perused by
us, would indicate that there was an inordinate delay of 10
hours in registration of the FIR. Though, the statement of
complainant  would  disclose  that  immediately  after  the
incident the appellant and Mr. Faizan were already at the
police station. In fact, the alleged half of a piece of brick
which is said to have been used by the appellant to assault
the deceased did not have any blood stains and as such
the  burden  would  be  on  the  prosecution  to  prove  the
alleged  overt  act  by  the  appellant  in  assaulting  the
deceased. Even the site plan (Najri Naksha) prepared by
the Investigating Officer (I.O) omits the presence of an eye-
witness.  The  complainant  is  the  person  on  whose
  SLP(Crl) Diary No(s). 36403/2026                                                                            2   

--- Page 157 ---
statement FIR came to be registered and as such, it is for
the prosecution to prove that the narrative is not post facto
concoction.
7. Having regard to the fact that appellant has already
been spent one a half year in custody and she being a lady.
We are of the considered view, that the proviso to 483 of
the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (“for short
BNSS”) would kick in to extend the benefit of granting the
bail.
8. Hence,  we  allow  this  appeal  and  set  aside  the
impugned order and direct her release by granting regular
bail,  subject  to  such  terms  and  conditions  as  the
jurisdictional Court may impose including the condition of
directing her to appear before the trial Court on all dates of
hearing  except  when  specifically  exempted  by  the  trial
Court.
9. It is also made clear that in the event of any of the
conditions imposed by the trial Court or by this Court is
violated, the respondent-State would be at liberty to seek
for cancellation of the bail by filing appropriate application
and in the event of such an application being filed, the
same  shall  be  considered  on  its  own  merits  and  in
  SLP(Crl) Diary No(s). 36403/2026                                                                            3   

--- Page 158 ---
accordance with law.
10. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
(Criminal Appeal No.      /2026)
(Arising out of SLP (Crl) No.   /2026)
(SLP (Criminal) Diary No. 31481/2026)
RAVINDRA KUMAR                        Appellant(s)
                      VERSUS
STATE OF BIHAR                      Respondent(s)
O R D E R
Heard.
     Delay condoned.
Leave granted. 
Appellant  who  has  been  arraigned  as  an
accused in FIR No. 63/2025 registered at Rajapakar
Police Station, District Vaishali Bihar, for the
offence punishable under Sections 25(1-B)(a), 26
and 35 of the Arms Act, 1959, is seeking for being
enlarged on bail.
1

--- Page 162 ---
It is the case of the prosecution that on the
mid-night  of  19.02.2025,  the  vehicle  checking
operation  was  going  on  and  appellant-Ravindra
Kumar and co-accused-Niraj Kumar were apprehended
after they attempted to flee and one 7.65 m.m
pistol with three live cartridges were recovered
from the appellant and Desi Katta with one live
cartridge was recovered from the co-accused.
The seizure memo does not disclose of any
independent witnesses having been associated with
seizure. The learned counsel appearing for the
respondent-State,  who  is  on  advance  notice,
vehemently opposed the grant of bail and he would
contend  that  there  are  22  cases  against  the
appellant and he is a habitual offender and if
released on bail, he is likely to indulge in
similar activities which would be a menace to the
society.  Hence,  the  learned  counsel  for  the
respondent-State  seeks  for  dismissal  of  the
appeal.
Per contra, learned counsel for the appellant
2

--- Page 163 ---
would  submit  that  on  account  of  appellant’s
brother having filed a complaint against one of
the police officers, has resulted in successive
FIRs being registered against the appellant and
his brother for petty offences and to keep the
appellant constantly behind the bars. He would
also submit that in all the cases which have been
filed, appellant has been granted bail and as such
he seeks for this appeal being allowed.
Having heard the learned counsels appearing
for the parties and on perusal of the records, it
would  emerge  therefrom  that  there  are  no
independent witnesses who have subscribed their
presence to the seizure memo. As to whether the
seizure was conducted in accordance with law or it
was  in  violation  of  Section  103  and  105  of
Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023 (“for
short BNSS”), as contended now is an issue which
requires to be examined after trial.
The fact that co-accused namely-Niraj Kumar,
who was also apprehended with the appellant having
3

--- Page 164 ---
been granted bail, we do not find any good ground
to deny the same to the appellant as he stands on
the same footing as that of Niraj Kumar. Hence, on
the ground of parity appellant is also entitled
for relief of bail.
Hence, we allow this appeal, set aside the
impugned order and direct the jurisdictional Court
to  release  the  appellant  on  such  terms  and
conditions as it deems fit including the condition
of  directing  him  to  appear  before  the
jurisdictional  Court  on  all  dates  of  hearing
except when specifically exempted for any specific
reason. 
Pending application(s), if any, shall stand
disposed of.

GARIMA DESWAL  ..... PETITIONER
              VERSUS
BRIJESH YADAV ..... RESPONDENT
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. In these proceedings wife has sought for transfer of the Divorce
Petition being HMA No.141/2025, titled as “ Brijesh Yadav v. Garima
Deswal”, filed under Section 13 of the Hindu Marriage Act, pending
before Family Court, Derra Bassi, Punjab to Family Court, Dwarka,
New Delhi.
3. This Court noticed that the possibility of settlement was
prevalent and as such referred the matter to the Supreme Court
Mediation Centre (SCMC). Both the parties have entered into a
settlement as per the report received from the Mediation Centre
along with the Settlement Agreement which has also been annexed as
Annexure A1 to the IA No.165332/2026 filed under Article 142 of the
Constitution of India read with Section 13B of the Hindu Marriage
Act, 1955. The parties have entered into a settlement and the terms
as agreed to between them reads as under:
“5. Both the parties hereto have arrived at an amicable
settlement on the following terms and conditions for
dissolution of marriage by mutual consent:-
1

--- Page 168 ---
A. That the parties have agreed that the Respondent-
husband will pay to the Petitioner-wife a total sum of
Rs. 16,00,000/- (Rupees Sixteen Lakhs Only) towards
full and final settlement of all her claims towards her
permanent  alimony,  Stridhan,  maintenance  (past,
present, future) and any other claim whatsoever.
B. That the Respondent/husband handed over 2 silver
coin, 1 Gold Chain, 1 Gold Ring, 1 Silver Ring to
Petitioner/wife.
C. It is agreed between the parties that they will move
an application jointly before the Hon'ble Supreme Court
under Article 142 of Constitution of India for invoking
inherent powers of the Hon'ble Supreme Court praying
for divorce by mutual consent as parties are staying
separately since 23.09.2022 as per SLP & 24.09.2022
according to Respondent i.e. for the last more than
four years and there is irretrievable break down of the
marriage.
D.  It is further agreed between the parties that if
Hon'ble Supreme Court is pleased to allow application
filed  by  both  the  parties  under  Article  142  of
Constitution of India then both the parties shall
withdraw all the cases filed by them against each
other.  The  Respondent  -husband  will  pay  to  the
Petitioner/ Wife a total sum of Rs. 16,00,000/- (Rupees
Sixteen Lakhs Only) via Demand Draft in the name of
Petitioner/wife during hearing of Application under
Article 142 of the Constitution of India.
AND/OR
In case this Hon'ble Court does not grant permission
under  Article  142  of  Constitution  of  India,  both
parties have agreed to file first motion before the
Competent Court at Delhi and the Respondent-husband
will pay amount of Rs. 16,00,000/- (Rupees Sixteen
Lakhs Only) in 2 installments is as under:-
I. The  Respondent-husband  shall  pay  first
installment an amount of Rs. 8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight
Lakhs only) in favour of the Petitioner/ wife by way of
demand draft at the time of First Motion.
II. The  Respondent-husband  shall  pay  second
2

--- Page 169 ---
installment an amount of Rs. 8,00,000/- (Rupees Eight
Lakhs only) in favour of the Petitioner/ wife by way of
demand draft at the time of Second Motion.
6.  That the Petitioner and the Respondent have agreed
that none of them will initiate any other legal action
or complaint against each other or against the family
members of each other in respect of their matrimonial
dispute in future.
7.  That subject to the aforesaid terms, the parties
have resolved all the disputes amicably in relation to

8. That by signing this Agreement the parties hereto
solemnly state and affirm that they have no further
claims  or  demands  against  each  other  including

all the disputes and differences have been amicably

Agreement, which have been arrived with free will of
the parties without any coercion, duress or collusion
and  parties  undertake  not  to  raise  any  dispute
whatsoever henceforth.”
4. Both the parties are present. This Court has interacted with the
parties who are present before Court. They have reiterated the
contents of the settlement agreement and have accepted that the
said agreement has been entered into voluntarily without any force,
threat or coercion and only after having understood the contents
thereto they have affixed their signatures. Learned counsels for
the parties who are present before this Court have also identified
the parties and in token of having identified them, they have
affixed their signatures to the settlement agreement. In view of
the same there is no impediment for accepting the settlement
agreement. Accordingly, it stands accepted.
3

--- Page 170 ---
5. Since, both the parties are well educated and knowing the
consequences of entering into the settlement and also having agreed
upon dissolution of marriage which came to be solemnized on
16.02.2020 as per Hindu rites and rituals and the chances of
reunion being remote and both the parties have consciously agreed
to part their ways, continuation of their marriage would be an
exercise in-futile. Hence, we are of the considered view that
dissolution of the marriage is the only course left open as they
are quite young and can carve out their future as they deem fit.
Accordingly, we accept the settlement entered into and marriage
solemnized between the petitioner and the respondent on 16.02.2020,
stands dissolved.
6. In the settlement agreement, the parties have also narrated the
different proceedings pending against each other as enumerated in
para 3(i) to 3(iv) and it reads as follows:
“3.  Whereas  the  Parties  have  filed  following  cases

(iv) Petitioner/wife has lodged FIR No. 0111/2025 dated

406 r/w 34 IPC.”

marriage having been dissolved, the continuation of aforesaid
4

--- Page 171 ---

quashed/set aside.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.         OF 2026  
(Arising out of SLP (Criminal) No. 5851 of 2024)
GHANSHYAM  APPELLANT(S)
VERSUS
THE STATE OF MADHYA PRADESH RESPONDENT(S)
WITH 
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.       OF 2026
(Arising out of SLP(Criminal) No. 10592/2024
O R D E R
1. Leave granted.
2. The present appeals arise out of the judgment(s)
dated 07.02.2024, passed by the High Court of Madhya
Pradesh at Indore in Criminal Appeal Nos. 1398 of 1998 and
343 of 1999.
3. Learned counsel for the appellant(s), at the outset,
has stated before this Court that the High Court, in
absence  of  counsel  for  the  appellant(s)  and  without
appointing an Amicus Curiae, has decided the matter, and
therefore, principles of natural justice and fair play have
been violated while convicting the appellant(s).
4. Learned counsel for the appellant(s) has placed

--- Page 190 ---
2
reliance upon the judgment delivered by this Court in case
of K. Muruganandam and Others v. State represented by the
Deputy Superintendent of Police and Another1. His contention
is that in light of the aforesaid judgment, the High Court
should have nominated an Amicus Curiae and, after taking
assistance  of  Amicus  Curiae,  should  have  passed  the
judgment.
5. After carefully gone through the record, we are of
the opinion that as the judgment has been delivered without
hearing the appellant(s) and as nobody has appeared on
their behalf, the judgment delivered in the matter deserves
to be set aside and is accordingly set aside.
6. The matters are remanded back to the High Court for
deciding the same afresh on merits after hearing the
parties.
7. In the present case, this Court on 19.04.2024 and
03.06.2024 has granted exemption from surrendering to the
appellant(s).
8. They were on bail during the pendency of the appeal
before the High Court. Accordingly, they shall continue to
remain on bail till the matter is finally decided by the
High Court. 
9. The appeals are disposed of in the above terms.

IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CRIMINAL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CRIMINAL APPEAL NO.3362 OF 2026
(@SLP(CRL.) NO.4899 OF 2026)
AMANDEEP SINGH CHANDOK ..... APPELLANT(S)
              VERSUS
STATE OF PUNJAB      ..... RESPONDENT(S)
O R D E R
1. Heard.
2. Leave granted.
3. An FIR No.0207/2025 for the offences punishable under
Section 318(4) and 61(2) of Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023
(BNS) came to be registered against the appellant and others
alleging  that  the  accused  in  connivance  with  an
impersonator, named, Satish Kumar induced the complainant to
enter  into  a  fraudulent  property  transaction,  obtained
original documents and thereby complainant had suffered a
wrongful  loss  to  the  tune  of  Rs.18  Lakhs.  The  role
attributed to appellant/accused is, he acted as a main
facilitator, orchestrated the transaction, introduced the
impersonator, secured property documents and subsequently
enabled the fraudulent transfer of property to a third
party.
 1                                                                              SLP(CRL.) NO.4899 OF 2026

--- Page 195 ---
4. It is not in dispute that there is a civil suit also
pending in respect of the present property in dispute and
the custodial interrogation of the appellant would not be
warranted, since allegations and counter allegations are to
be evaluated, examined and investigated by the Investigating
Officer (IO) on the basis of the documents. It is contended
by the learned counsel appearing for the respondent-State
that the said suit has been dismissed for default. However,
we shall not go into the said aspect. It is for the parties
to take steps, if so advised.  Even otherwise by directing
the appellant to appear before the IO, as it would suffice
to insulate any steps if taken by the accused to derail the
investigation.
5. In that view of the matter, we allow the appeal and set
aside  the  impugned  order.  Appellant  is  ordered  to  be
released on anticipatory bail on such terms and conditions
as the jurisdictional IO may deem fit to impose including
the condition of directing the appellant to appear before
the IO not only as and when called upon but also once a week
viz; every Thursday between 10:00 am to 02:00 pm till filing
of the chargesheet and also on the condition that appellant
would appear before the jurisdictional trial court on all
dates of hearing except when exempted for any specific
reason.
 2                                                                              SLP(CRL.) NO.4899 OF 2026

--- Page 196 ---
6. Pending application(s), if any, shall stand disposed of.

Hence, she lodged the complaint for suitable action being taken
against the appellant.

2. Mr. Mukul Rohatgi, learned Senior counsel for the

3. The petitioner thereafter being aggrieved by order
dated 15.06.2026, preferred a petition for grant of regular
bail before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana and the
same was registered as CRM-M-34651/2026 (O & M). Notices
were issued in the matter on 07.07.2026 and High Court
directed the matter to be listed on 05.08.2026.
4. It has been further stated than an application was
also preferred for grant of interim bail and a request was
made to the High Court to hear the application, however,
the mentioning was declined. There is no order on record
that the mentioning was declined in the matter.
5. The petitioner thereafter preferred a special leave
petition before this Court for grant of bail. It was
submitted before this Court that the High Court was not
hearing the matter. In those circumstances, by order dated
20.07.2026, and keeping in view the statement made by the
learned  senior  counsel  for  the  petitioner  that  the
petitioner is unwell, Mr. Suryaprakash V. Raju, learned
